newsitem.title: USA: NJ bond plan passes first test, faces Monday vote.
newsitem.headline: NJ bond plan passes first test, faces Monday vote.

text.p: New Jersey Gov. Christine Whitman's plan to sell $2.9 billion of pension bonds passed its first legislative test Thursday, and is expected to handle its next hurdle just as easily.
The Assembly Appropriations Committee late Thursday approved a bill empowering the state to borrow $2.9 billion to eliminate the unfunded liability in its pension funds.

The 8-5 party-line vote followed a marathon hearing, in which Treasurer Brian Clymer urged legislators to act, not debate. He said time was of the essence because interest rates may not be so favorable in a few months.

The full Assembly is expected to vote on the measure Monday, and it is not expected to face any difficulties. A stiffer test awaits in the state Senate, however, where support even among the governor's Republican allies has been questioned.
Opposition Democrats said a reasonable financial management tool was being "distorted" to enable Republican Gov. Christie Whitman to avoid $647 million in pension fund contributions.

The essence of the borrowing proposal is to make a lump sum payment into the pension funds, instead of reducing unfunded liabilities with small annual payments that add up to a much greater total over the long-term.
The lump sum can be borrowed at an estimated 7.5 percent interest rate, while the state's investment portfolio is expected to earn 8.75 percent and has earned 12.3 percent over the last decade.
The law voted out of committee Thursday empowers the state to use "excess value" in the funds to reduce annual contributions. It was amended to end that practice in 2004.
